60: That looks like the GPU running out of headroom, when it is really the same prefill computed twice.
61: 👉 Every engine ships continuous batching under a different name: vLLM, SGLang, and TGI call it that, TensorRT-LLM calls it in-flight batching, LMDeploy calls it persistent batching.
63: Rebuilding the batch every pass fixes the slow-member problem and introduces a new one, which users see as a stutter.
64: A joining request is prefilled in one iteration. A 32K-token prompt is one large, compute-heavy pass that every active decode waits behind, so output pauses mid-sentence because someone else pasted a long document.
65: Here's how things look without and with chunked prefill.
68: (prompt of request C is broken down into smaller chunks of 2k tokens each)
69: Split the prompt across iterations. Chunked prefill breaks the prompt into fixed-size token ranges scheduled over several passes, each extending the request's KV cache.
70: The attention math is unchanged, since later chunks attend to what earlier chunks processed. The first token arrives after the final chunk.
71: Prefill is compute bound and decode is memory bound, so one batch containing both uses both parts of the chip.
73: Smaller chunks give the scheduler more opportunities to run decodes, reducing ITL spikes for active requests.
74: Larger chunks process the new prompt more efficiently and usually improve the TTFT, but active decodes may wait longer between tokens.
75: Chunks that are too small can lower GPU utilization and add attention overhead because later chunks must reread KV cache entries created by earlier chunks.
76: Chunked prefill is on by default in vLLM V1, where --max-num-batched-tokens caps tokens per iteration. SGLang uses --chunked-prefill-size, and -1 disables it.
79: 👉 There is no universal best chunk size. It depends on the model, the GPU, your prompt length distribution, and which latency metric your SLO measures.
81: The three strategies differ only in when they fix the batch, and each answers a different workload shape.
82: For live traffic with variable output lengths, continuous batching is the only one that holds up, and every major engine gives it to you by default.
83: This whole article rests on one fact about GPUs: a forward pass is bottlenecked on reading weights out of memory, not on the math.
